Class-based views live in `src/tessel/views.py`. `VerbView` is the one that maps HTTP methods to `get()` and `post()`. It sits on top of the generic `View`.

## Classes and methods

- `View` (`views.py:16`) has the classmethod `to_view_func()` (line 86), which turns the class into a plain function.
- `VerbView(View)` (`views.py:138`) has `__init_subclass__` (line 165) and `run_view` (line 182).
- `http_method_funcs` (`views.py:11`) is the set of recognised method names: get, query, post, head, options, delete, put, trace, patch.

## Step by step

1. **Class creation computes `methods`.** When you subclass `VerbView`, `__init_subclass__` runs (line 165). Unless the subclass sets `methods` itself, it collects:
   - methods inherited from base classes' `methods`, and
   - the upper-cased name of every entry in `http_method_funcs` that the class has (`hasattr`).

   A class with `get` and `post` gets `methods = {"GET", "POST"}` (lines 168–180).

2. **Build the view function.** `MyView.to_view_func("name")` (line 86) creates a closure `view(**kwargs)`:
   - By default (`init_every_request = True`) it creates a new instance of the class per request, using `view.view_class(*class_args, **class_kwargs)`, and then calls `self.run_view`.
   - If `init_every_request = False`, it creates one instance up front and reuses it (line 113).
   - In both cases the call goes through `active_app.ensure_sync(...)`, so async methods also work.

3. **Decorate and tag.** Any `decorators` on the class are applied in order (lines 118–122). The function then gets these attributes (lines 129–134):
   - `view_class`, the class itself;
   - `__name__`, `__doc__` and `__module__`;
   - `methods`, copied from the class;
   - `provide_automatic_options`.

4. **Register the route.** `app.attach_route_rule("/x", view_func=MyView.to_view_func("x"))` passes the function to `Tessel.attach_route_rule` (`src/tessel/sansio/app.py:606`). That reads `view_func.methods` (line 623) and so builds the `Rule` with exactly `GET` and `POST`, adding `OPTIONS` if automatic options are on.

5. **Request time, routing.** Werkzeug only matches the URL rule for the allowed methods, so a method that isn't defined is rejected with 405 before any view code runs. `Tessel.run_view` (`src/tessel/app.py:966`) then calls the stored view function with the URL variables.

6. **Request time, dispatch.** `view(**kwargs)` calls `VerbView.run_view` (line 182). That does `getattr(self, request.method.lower(), None)`, finding `get` or `post` on the instance, and calls it with the URL variables as keyword arguments. `request` is the context proxy described earlier.

7. **HEAD fallback.** If the request is `HEAD` and the class has no `head`, it falls back to `get` (lines 187–188). Note that `__init_subclass__` only adds `HEAD` to `methods` if the class defines `head`, so a `HEAD` request for a class with only `get` relies on the app's default method handling at the routing layer rather than on `methods`. I haven't confirmed how that interacts with the `Rule` here.

8. **Missing handler.** If no handler is found, the `assert` on line 190 fails. This only happens when `methods` was set manually to include a verb the class doesn't implement.
